listeningParts.title: Booking a sea-kayaking trip
listeningParts.contextDescription: A woman phones a coastal activity centre to book a group kayaking trip.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, Harbourside Paddle Centre, this is Owen. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Oh, hello. I'm organising a day out for a group from my office and somebody recommended your sea-kayaking trips. I wondered if I could book one, or at least find out a bit more.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Of course. We run two kinds of trip at the moment: the Bay Explorer, which stays inside the harbour wall, and the Cliff Coast trip, which goes out along the headland. Has anyone in your group paddled before?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hardly anyone. Maybe two people have tried it on holiday, but the rest are complete beginners.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Then I'd definitely suggest the Bay Explorer. The water's calmer and the guides spend the first forty minutes on the beach teaching the basic strokes. The Cliff Coast trip is only for people who can already do a rescue.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The Bay Explorer sounds right. How long does it last?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: It used to be a three-hour session, but since the spring we've made it four hours, because people kept asking for more time on the water. That includes a break for lunch on the island.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Lovely. And what does it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: It's forty-two pounds per person. Groups of ten or more get a discount, so it comes down to thirty-eight each.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: There'll be twelve of us, so that's good news. Can I take your details? Sorry, I mean, can I give you mine so you can make the booking?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, please. What's your name?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Priya Venkat. That's V-E-N-K-A-T.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you. And which date were you thinking of?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: We'd originally said Friday the fourteenth of June, but half the team are at a conference that day, so could we do Saturday the fifteenth instead?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Let me check... yes, the fifteenth is fine. Morning or afternoon?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Morning, I think. Then people can go home and rest.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Sensible. Meet at nine-thirty, but please don't be late, because the tide sets our start time and we launch at ten o'clock exactly.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Understood. Where exactly do we meet? Is it at your office on the high street?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: No, the office is just for bookings. You meet us at the boathouse, which is the green building at the end of Quay Road, next to the lifeboat station.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Quay Road. Got it. What do people need to bring? I suppose you provide the kayaks.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: We provide kayaks, paddles, buoyancy aids and wetsuits. People should bring a towel, a change of clothes and some old trainers that they don't mind getting wet. Flip-flops aren't allowed because they come off in the water.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Trainers, not flip-flops. And lunch?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Lunch is included in the price. It's a picnic from the café: sandwiches, fruit and a hot drink. If anyone has dietary requirements, just let us know at least a week before.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: One colleague is vegan, so I'll mention that now if that's all right.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: That's fine, I'll put a note on the booking. Now, is there anything else we should know about the group? Any medical conditions, for example?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Not that I know of. But one person is quite nervous about deep water.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: That happens a lot. We can put her in a double kayak with one of the guides, so she won't need to steer. Just tell her to talk to the lead guide when she arrives.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's reassuring. How do I pay?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: We take a deposit now to hold the date, and the rest on the day. The deposit is twenty per cent of the total.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Fine. And what happens if the weather's bad?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: If the wind is too strong, we'll phone you by seven a.m. on the day and either move you to another date or give you a full refund. You don't lose anything.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Perfect. And is there parking?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: There's a pay-and-display car park behind the boathouse, but it fills up quickly on Saturdays in summer. A lot of groups share a minibus, or you can take the number 7 bus, which stops right outside.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'll suggest the bus. Thank you so much, Owen, you've been really helpful.

listeningParts.title: Visiting the tidal energy centre
listeningParts.contextDescription: A guide welcomes visitors to a tidal energy visitor centre and explains the site and the technology.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Strangford Point Tidal Energy Centre. My name's Aoife and I'll be looking after you for the next hour or so. Before we set off, I'd like to give you a quick idea of how the site is laid out, so please have a look at the plan in your leaflet.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: We're standing in the entrance hall, at the bottom of the plan. Straight ahead of you, through the glass doors, is the main exhibition, and that's where we'll start. On your right as you came in, you'll have noticed the shop. Next to the shop, in the bottom right-hand corner, are the toilets and the lockers, if you want to leave your bags.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Now, the café. A lot of people expect it to be near the entrance, but in fact it's at the far end of the building, in the top left-hand corner, because it has the best view over the water. If you follow the corridor along the left-hand side past the lecture theatre, you'll come to it.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The lecture theatre itself is the large room on the left, between the entrance hall and the café. We'll be showing a short film there at eleven. The control room, which is the heart of the whole operation, is in the middle of the building, directly behind the exhibition. You can't go inside, I'm afraid, but there's a window along the corridor where you can watch the engineers at work.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Finally, the viewing platform. To reach it, go through the door at the end of the exhibition on the right-hand side and climb the outside stairs. The platform sits right at the top right-hand corner of the site, above the sea wall, and from there you can see the marker buoys that show where the turbines are.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: So, a few words about the centre itself. Many visitors assume the turbines produce electricity only when the tide is coming in. In fact, the blades can turn in either direction, so they generate power on the incoming tide and the outgoing tide. The only times they stop are the short periods at high water and low water, when the current is too slow.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: People also ask why we chose this spot. Wave height isn't really the issue for tidal power, and the water here isn't especially deep. What makes Strangford Point special is the narrow channel: when the tide pushes a huge volume of water through a gap this small, the current speeds up enormously, and fast water is what a turbine needs.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: There are currently six turbines on the seabed, each about the height of a three-storey house. Together, on an average day, they supply enough electricity for around four thousand homes. That's less than a large wind farm, of course, but the advantage is that we know exactly when the tides will come, years in advance. Wind and sunshine can't be predicted like that, so the grid operator values our output highly.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Of course, there are concerns. When the project began, local fishermen were worried that the turbines would harm fish and seals. So, for the first three years, an independent team from the university fitted cameras and sonar to the turbines. They found that seals tended to avoid the blades completely, and there was no measurable fall in fish numbers. Monitoring still continues, but on a smaller scale.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The biggest challenge has actually been maintenance. Saltwater is very hard on machinery, and divers can only work safely during the slack water I mentioned, which might be just forty minutes. So the newer turbines are designed so that the whole unit can be lifted out of the water by a ship and repaired in the harbour. That's far cheaper and safer than sending divers down.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: And what about the future? The company would like to add more turbines, but before that happens, the cable that takes the electricity to shore needs to be replaced with a larger one. That work is planned for next year. Right, let's go through to the exhibition.

listeningParts.title: Planning a microplastics project
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two marine science students, Leon and Hana, discuss their research project with their tutor, Dr Morris.

dialogue.speaker: Dr Morris
dialogue.text: Come in, both of you. So, you've been working on the outline for your microplastics project. How's it going?

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: Pretty well, I think. We've decided to compare the amount of microplastics in sand at two beaches: the town beach near the river mouth and the beach at Kelly Bay, which is much more remote.

dialogue.speaker: Dr Morris
dialogue.text: That's a nice clear comparison. What do you expect to find?

dialogue.speaker: Leon
dialogue.text: Well, my first thought was that the town beach would have far more, because of all the visitors. But Hana pointed out that the river probably matters more than the tourists. A lot of plastic fibres come from washing machines, and they travel down the river into the sea.

dialogue.speaker: Dr Morris
dialogue.text: Good. So your hypothesis is about the river rather than the beach users. Make sure that's stated clearly in your introduction. Now, how are you planning to collect the samples?

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: We'll mark out squares on the beach, half a metre on each side, and take the top five centimetres of sand from each one. We were going to sample just along the high-tide line, where you can actually see rubbish collecting.

dialogue.speaker: Dr Morris
dialogue.text: Hmm. The trouble is that the high-tide line changes from day to day. I'd suggest you take samples at three distances from the water instead: the high-tide line, the middle of the beach and the back near the dunes. Then you can see whether the particles are spread evenly.

dialogue.speaker: Leon
dialogue.text: That would triple the number of samples, though. Is that realistic?

dialogue.speaker: Dr Morris
dialogue.text: If you cut the number of squares at each distance from ten to five, it's about the same amount of work. And you'll have a much more interesting result.

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: Okay, that makes sense. The other thing we wanted to ask about was contamination. We've read that people's clothes can shed fibres into the samples.

dialogue.speaker: Dr Morris
dialogue.text: Yes, it's a real problem in this field. The simplest solution is to wear cotton lab coats and leave a clean dish of filtered water open beside you while you work. Anything that lands in that dish tells you how much contamination there is, and you can subtract it from your results.

dialogue.speaker: Leon
dialogue.text: That's clever. We hadn't thought of measuring it rather than just trying to avoid it.

dialogue.speaker: Dr Morris
dialogue.text: Now, your reading. Which sources have you looked at so far?

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: Quite a few. The government report on coastal pollution was useful for background, but honestly, it's ten years old, so a lot of the figures are out of date.

dialogue.speaker: Leon
dialogue.text: Then there's the Thompson study. I found it really useful because she explains her laboratory method step by step, so we could almost copy her procedure for separating plastics from sand.

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: I wasn't so sure about Thompson. Her sample was very small, only two beaches, like ours. I preferred the review by Castillo, which brings together results from more than sixty studies around the world.

dialogue.speaker: Dr Morris
dialogue.text: Castillo is excellent for comparison. You could use her figures to say whether your beaches are typical. What about the article in the newspaper you mentioned in your email?

dialogue.speaker: Leon
dialogue.text: Oh, that one. It had some striking photographs, but when I checked, the numbers it quoted didn't seem to come from any published research.

dialogue.speaker: Dr Morris
dialogue.text: Then leave it out. A newspaper can give you an idea, but it isn't evidence. And the citizen science website?

dialogue.speaker: Hana
dialogue.text: The Beach Watch site. Volunteers all over the country record what they find. The data isn't as precise as a lab study, but there's an enormous amount of it, and it's updated every month, so it's the most current source we have.

dialogue.speaker: Dr Morris
dialogue.text: Exactly. Use it, but explain its limitations. Right, I'd like a draft of your method section by next Thursday, please.

listeningParts.title: A short history of wind power
listeningParts.contextDescription: Part of a lecture in an engineering history course.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. Today we're continuing our series on energy history, and I want to look at wind power. We tend to think of wind turbines as a modern technology, but people have been using the wind to do work for well over a thousand years.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The earliest windmills that we have clear records of were built in Persia, in what is now eastern Iran, probably in the ninth century. These looked very different from the windmills most of us picture. The sails were arranged around a vertical shaft, a bit like a revolving door, and they were surrounded by walls that directed the wind onto one side. Their main job was grinding grain, though some were also used to pump water for irrigation.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In Europe, windmills appear in the late twelfth century, and these had a horizontal shaft, with the sails facing into the wind. The early European design was called the post mill, because the whole wooden body of the mill sat on a single large post. When the wind changed direction, the miller had to push the entire building round to face it, using a long beam at the back. As you can imagine, that limited how big a post mill could be.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The solution was the tower mill. Here, the body was a fixed tower of stone or brick, and only the cap at the top, which carried the sails, needed to turn. That meant the mills could be much taller, catching stronger winds. Then, in the eighteenth century, an English inventor added the fantail: a small wheel at the back of the cap that automatically turned the sails into the wind. The miller no longer had to watch the weather all day.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Now, the place where windmills had their greatest impact was probably the Netherlands. A large part of the country lies below sea level, and from the fifteenth century onwards, thousands of windmills were used for drainage, pumping water out of the land so that it could be farmed. By the mid-nineteenth century, there were around nine thousand windmills in the country. They also powered sawmills, which helped the Dutch build the ships that made them a major trading nation.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Windmills declined in the late nineteenth century, when steam engines, and later electric motors, became cheap and reliable. But the idea of using wind to make electricity is older than many people realise. In 1887, a Scottish professor, James Blyth, built a wind turbine in the garden of his holiday cottage and used it to charge batteries that lit the house. Local people apparently refused his offer to light the main street, because they thought electricity was the work of the devil.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In the United States, small wind turbines were common on farms in the 1920s and 1930s, before the national electricity grid reached rural areas. Once farms were connected to the grid, most of these turbines were abandoned. So for much of the twentieth century, wind power was seen as a curiosity, something for remote places only.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: What changed that? The oil crisis of the 1970s. When oil prices rose sharply, governments began to look for other sources of energy, and Denmark in particular invested heavily in wind research. Danish engineers settled on the design you now see everywhere: three blades, facing into the wind, on a tall steel tower. Three blades turned out to be the best balance between efficiency and stability. Two-bladed turbines wobble more as they turn, and four or more blades add weight and cost without producing much extra power.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Since then, the main trend has simply been size. A typical turbine in the 1980s had blades about fifteen metres long. Today, the largest offshore turbines have blades of over a hundred metres, and a single rotation can power an average home for a couple of days. Moving out to sea has been important, because the wind there is stronger and steadier, and turbines don't face the same opposition from people who object to the view.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: However, size brings its own problems. Blades this long are extremely difficult to transport by road, and at the end of their life, they're hard to recycle, because they're made from a mixture of glass fibre and resin. Several companies are now developing blades that can be broken down and reused, and that, I think, will be one of the key challenges of the next decade. Next week, we'll move on to solar energy.

readingPassages.title: The return of the sail
paragraphs: For most of human history, ships crossed the oceans by sail. Then, in the nineteenth century, steam engines and later diesel engines made sailing ships seem hopelessly old-fashioned. A motor ship could keep to a timetable regardless of the weather, and by the 1930s commercial sail had almost disappeared. Today, around ninety per cent of world trade travels by sea, and almost all of it is carried by ships burning heavy fuel oil. Shipping produces roughly three per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions, about the same as a large industrial country, and international rules now require the industry to cut those emissions sharply by the middle of the century.

One of the more surprising responses to this pressure is the return of wind power. Engineers are not proposing a return to the clipper ships of the past, which needed large crews to handle hundreds of square metres of canvas. Instead, they are developing what is known as wind-assisted propulsion: equipment fitted to ordinary cargo ships that uses the wind to reduce, rather than replace, the work done by the engine. Because the engine remains on board, the ship can still keep to its schedule when the wind drops. Crucially, most of these systems are largely automated, so they do not require additional crew members, which would quickly cancel out any savings on fuel.

Several technologies are competing. The oldest of them, the rotor sail, was first tested in the 1920s by the German engineer Anton Flettner. It consists of a tall vertical cylinder that is spun by a small electric motor. When wind blows across the spinning cylinder, the air moves faster on one side than the other, creating a difference in pressure that pushes the ship forward. This is the same effect that makes a football curve when it is kicked with spin. Flettner's rotor ship crossed the Atlantic in 1926, but the low price of oil at the time meant that there was little commercial interest in the idea.

A second approach uses rigid wing sails, which look rather like aircraft wings standing on end. Made of composite materials, they can be angled automatically by computer to make the best use of the wind, and some designs can be folded down when the ship enters port or passes under a bridge. A third option, the kite, is perhaps the most unusual: a large parafoil flies several hundred metres above the ship, where winds are stronger and more constant, and pulls the vessel along by a cable attached to the bow.

How much fuel can these devices save? The answer depends heavily on the route and the type of ship. Trials on vessels fitted with rotor sails have reported fuel savings of between five and twenty per cent, and developers claim that wing sails could achieve more than that on routes with steady winds, such as parts of the North Atlantic. Routes through regions with weak or unpredictable winds offer much smaller gains. Critics also point out that many published figures come from the manufacturers themselves, and independent long-term data is still limited.

There are practical obstacles as well. Rotors and wing sails take up deck space, which on a container ship is valuable, since every container that cannot be carried represents lost income. Tall structures can also interfere with the cranes used to load and unload ships in port. For this reason, early adopters have mostly been bulk carriers and tankers, which carry cargo inside the hull and have relatively clear decks. Ship owners must also weigh the cost of installation, which can run into millions of dollars per vessel, against uncertain future fuel prices.

Despite these difficulties, interest is growing quickly. In the past decade, the number of large ships fitted with some form of wind-assisted propulsion has risen from a handful to several dozen, and many more are on order. Some analysts believe that the greatest benefit will come from combining wind power with other measures, such as slower sailing speeds and improved hull designs. Even a saving of ten per cent, multiplied across tens of thousands of ships, would represent a significant cut in global emissions. After a century in the background, the wind may be returning to the centre of world trade.

readingPassages.title: Meadows beneath the sea
paragraphs: Seagrasses are often mistaken for seaweed, but the two are quite different. Seaweeds are algae, which absorb nutrients directly from the water through their surfaces. Seagrasses, by contrast, are true flowering plants, related to the grasses and lilies that grow on land. They have roots, leaves and veins, and they produce flowers and seeds, all underwater. Around seventy species are found in shallow coastal waters on every continent except Antarctica, where they form dense green meadows that can stretch for many kilometres.

These meadows are among the most productive habitats on Earth. A single hectare of seagrass can support tens of thousands of fish and millions of small invertebrates, and many commercially important species, including cod and some kinds of prawn, spend the early part of their lives sheltering among the leaves. Seagrass is also the main food of animals such as dugongs and green turtles. One study estimated that a fifth of the world's largest fisheries depend on seagrass meadows at some stage of the life cycle of the fish they catch.

In recent years, however, it is the role of seagrass in tackling climate change that has attracted most attention. Like all plants, seagrasses take carbon dioxide from the atmosphere as they grow. What makes them unusual is what happens to that carbon. The dense leaves slow the movement of water, so fine particles settle on the seabed, and the roots bind these sediments together. Because the sediment contains little oxygen, dead plant material decays very slowly, and carbon can remain locked in the seabed for centuries or even thousands of years. Although seagrass covers less than 0.2 per cent of the ocean floor, it is thought to be responsible for around ten per cent of the carbon buried in ocean sediments each year.

Unfortunately, seagrass is disappearing. A global assessment published in 2009 concluded that around seven per cent of the world's meadows were being lost every year, a rate comparable to the destruction of tropical rainforests. The causes are varied. Fertiliser and sewage washing off the land encourage the growth of algae, which cloud the water and block the sunlight that seagrass needs. Dredging, boat anchors and coastal construction physically tear up meadows, and in some places disease has killed large areas. When seagrass dies, the sediment it was holding can be washed away, releasing stored carbon back into the water.

Restoring lost meadows has proved difficult. Early attempts involved digging up plants from healthy meadows and replanting them elsewhere, but this damaged the donor sites and many transplants failed. Researchers at the University of Virginia took a different approach in the coastal bays of the eastern United States, where seagrass had been wiped out by disease and a hurricane in the 1930s. Beginning in 1999, they scattered more than seventy million seeds over the bare seabed. Progress was slow at first, but the meadows eventually began to spread by themselves, and today they cover more than three thousand six hundred hectares. The project's leader, Professor Robert Orth, has described the result as evidence that 'if you give nature a helping hand, it can do remarkable things'.

Elsewhere, projects have adopted other methods. In Wales, a project known as Seagrass Ocean Rescue collected seeds by hand, with the help of volunteer divers, and planted them in small hessian bags filled with sand, which were then lowered onto the seabed in rows. Marine biologist Dr Richard Unsworth, one of the project's founders, argues that local involvement is just as important as the technique: in his view, a meadow is far more likely to survive if the surrounding community understands its value and supports efforts to reduce pollution.

Not all scientists are convinced that restoration should be the priority. Dr Carlos Duarte, who has studied seagrass for decades, has pointed out that protecting existing meadows is far cheaper and more reliable than creating new ones, since a damaged meadow may take decades to recover its full carbon store. Others warn against treating seagrass simply as a way to cancel out emissions, a concern raised by the economist Dr Lena Fischer, who fears that companies might pay for planting projects instead of reducing their own pollution. What most experts agree on is that seagrass deserves far more attention than it has received in the past.

readingPassages.title: Why we misjudge our energy use
paragraphs: If you ask people how much energy different household activities use, their answers are often surprisingly inaccurate. In a well-known study in the United States, the psychologist Shahzeen Attari asked several hundred participants to estimate the energy used by everyday devices and activities, from running a dishwasher to drying clothes. On average, participants underestimated energy use by a factor of almost three. More strikingly, the errors were not random. People slightly overestimated the energy used by small, visible devices such as light bulbs, but dramatically underestimated the energy used by large appliances, particularly those that produce heat, such as water heaters and tumble dryers.

Why should this be? One explanation lies in the way people make judgements when they lack precise information. Rather than calculating, they rely on mental shortcuts, and one of the most common is to judge the size of something by how noticeable it is. A light is switched on and off many times a day; it is in plain view, and we are constantly reminded to turn it off. A water heater, by contrast, sits out of sight in a cupboard and works silently. It is therefore easy to assume that the light matters more, even though heating water typically uses many times as much energy.

A second factor is that energy is, for most people, invisible. When we buy food or petrol, we see exactly how much we are getting, and the price is displayed at the moment of purchase. Electricity and gas, however, arrive continuously through wires and pipes, and the bill comes weeks later as a single figure that combines dozens of activities. It is almost impossible to connect a particular choice, such as taking a longer shower, with its cost. Economists describe this as a problem of feedback: without clear and timely information about the consequences of our actions, we cannot learn to adjust them.

This analysis suggests an obvious remedy: give people better feedback. In recent years, millions of homes in Europe and North America have been fitted with smart meters, which can display energy use in real time on a small screen in the kitchen. Early trials produced encouraging results, with some households cutting their consumption by ten per cent or more. However, larger and longer studies have generally found smaller effects, typically around two or three per cent. One reason appears to be that the novelty wears off: many people look at their display frequently in the first few weeks, and then rarely, if ever. In my view, this does not mean that feedback is useless, but rather that simply providing data is not enough.

Some of the most effective interventions have combined information with social comparison. In a series of experiments, an American energy company sent customers letters that compared their consumption with that of similar neighbours, adding a smiling face for those who used less than average. Households receiving these letters reduced their energy use by around two per cent, a small figure for an individual home, but a large one across a whole country, and achieved at very low cost. Interestingly, the researchers found that households who were already using less than their neighbours sometimes increased their consumption after learning this, an effect that was reduced when the letters included the smiling face.

Defaults offer another powerful tool. Psychologists have long known that people tend to accept whatever option is presented as standard. In one German study, when a town's electricity supplier made green energy the default tariff, so that customers had to take action to switch away from it, more than ninety per cent of households stayed with it, even though it was slightly more expensive. When the same option had to be chosen actively, only a small minority selected it. Critics argue that such techniques can be manipulative, but I believe that when the default is clearly explained and easy to change, it simply makes the sustainable choice the easy one.

None of this means that behaviour change alone can solve the problem of energy demand. Better insulation, more efficient appliances and cleaner sources of electricity will matter far more in the long run. But buildings and appliances are used by people, and the way they are used depends on what people understand and notice. Policies that ignore human psychology are likely to deliver less than their designers expect, while those that take it into account may achieve a great deal at surprisingly little cost.
